question: When can an agency award a contract without full and open competition because only one source can do the work?
key_facts: only one responsible source
answer: An agency may award without full and open competition when the supplies or services are available from only one responsible source (or, for DoD/NASA/Coast Guard, only one or a limited number) and no other type of supplies or services will satisfy the agency’s requirements [1][2]. Examples include: a unique unsolicited research proposal that (A) demonstrates a unique and innovative concept or capability, (B) offers a concept or services not otherwise available to the Government, and (C) does not resemble a pending competitive acquisition [1][8]; follow‑on contracts for continued development or production of a major system or highly specialized equipment (or, for DoD/NASA/Coast Guard, continued provision of highly specialized services) when other awards would cause substantial duplication of cost not expected to be recovered or unacceptable delays [1]. Limitations and required actions: the award must be supported by the written justification and approvals in 6.303 and 6.304 and the synopsis/notice and any bids/proposals/capability statements must have been considered [3]; the authority should not be used when other 6.302 authorities apply and may not be justified by lack of advance planning or funding concerns, and the CO must solicit offers from as many potential sources as practicable [4][6]. Brand‑name specifications that preclude competition also require J&A and posting as described in 6.302‑1(c) [6]. Additionally, when deciding multiple vs. single awards under indefinite‑quantity contracts, the CO must consider whether only one contractor is capable of performing because supplies/services are unique or highly specialized [7].

question: How long can a contract awarded under unusual and compelling urgency last?
key_facts: may not exceed one year including options, unless head of agency determines exceptional circumstances
answer: The total period of performance “may not exceed one year, including all options,” unless the head of the agency determines that exceptional circumstances apply (that determination must be documented in the contract file). The period also may not exceed the time necessary to (A) meet the unusual and compelling requirements of the work and (B) for the agency to enter into another contract for the required goods and services through the use of competitive procedures. Any subsequent modification that will extend the cumulative period beyond one year requires a separate, like-level approval/determination. [1]

question: Who has to approve a justification for other than full and open competition, and how does it depend on dollar value?
key_facts: tiered approval up to the senior procurement executive
answer:
Approval authorities for justifications for other than full and open competition are set by dollar thresholds as follows: 
- For a proposed contract not exceeding $900,000, the contracting officer’s certification required by 6.303-2(b)(12) serves as approval unless agency procedures establish a higher approving level [1][3].
- For a proposed contract over $900,000 but not exceeding $20 million, approval must be by the advocate for competition for the procuring activity designated pursuant to 6.501 or by an official described in 6.304(a)(3) or (4); this authority is not delegable [1].
- For a proposed contract over $20 million but not exceeding $90 million (or, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, not exceeding $150 million), approval must be by the head of the procuring activity or a designee who—if military, is a general or flag officer; or—if civilian, is serving in a grade above GS‑15 (or comparable) [1].
- For a proposed contract over $90 million (or, for DoD, NASA, and the Coast Guard, over $150 million), approval must be by the agency’s senior procurement executive designated pursuant to 41 U.S.C. 1702(c); this authority is not delegable except as specified for the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment for DoD [1].
Additional points: any justification for a contract awarded under 6.302-7 is considered approved when the determination required by 6.302-7(c)(1) is made (regardless of dollar amount) [1]. Class justifications are approved in writing in accordance with agency procedures, with approval level determined by the estimated total value of the class, and the estimated dollar value of all options must be included in determining approval level [1]. Contracting officers must obtain the approval required by 6.304 before proceeding as required by 6.303-1 [3].

question: What must a justification for other than full and open competition contain?
key_facts: list of required contents incl. description of supplies/services, authority cited
answer: The justification must contain sufficient facts and rationale to justify the use of the specific authority cited (6.303-2(a)) and, as a minimum (except for sole‑source 8(a) contracts over $30 million), must include: (1) identification of the agency and contracting activity and specific identification of the document as a “Justification for other than full and open competition”; (2) nature/description of the action being approved; (3) a description of the supplies or services required (including the estimated value); (4) identification of the statutory authority permitting other than full and open competition; (5) a demonstration that the proposed contractor’s unique qualifications or the nature of the acquisition requires use of the cited authority; (6) a description of efforts made to ensure offers were solicited from as many potential sources as practicable (including notice/publicity or which 5.202 exception applies); (7) a contracting officer determination that the anticipated cost to the Government will be fair and reasonable; (8) a description of market research conducted and results or a statement why market research was not conducted; (9) any other supporting facts such as why technical data/specifications are not available, estimates of duplicated cost for follow‑on acquisitions when 6.302‑1 is cited, or harm rationale when 6.302‑2 is cited; (10) a listing of sources that expressed written interest; (11) actions the agency may take to remove or overcome competition barriers before any subsequent acquisition; and (12) contracting officer certification that the justification is accurate and complete to the contracting officer’s knowledge and belief (6.303‑2(b)). Additionally, the justification must include evidence that supporting data provided by technical or requirements personnel and forming a basis for the justification have been certified as complete and accurate by those personnel (6.303‑2(c)). For sole‑source 8(a) contracts over $30 million, the justification must instead include: (1) a description of the agency’s needs covered by the contract; (2) specification of the statutory provision providing the exception to competitive procedures; (3) a determination that use of a sole‑source contract is in the agency’s best interest; (4) a determination that the anticipated cost will be fair and reasonable; and (5) such other matters as the head of the agency specifies (6.303‑2(d)).

question: What is the micro-purchase threshold?
key_facts: $15,000 (with exceptions)
answer: The micro-purchase threshold is $15,000. For acquisitions of construction subject to 40 U.S.C. chapter 31, subchapter IV, Wage Rate Requirements (Construction), the threshold is $2,000 [8].

question: What is the simplified acquisition threshold?
key_facts: $350,000 (with exceptions)
answer: The provided sources do not state the base dollar amount for the simplified acquisition threshold. They do state that for acquisitions of commercial products and commercial services using subpart 13.5 the applicable limit is $9 million ($15 million for acquisitions as described in 13.500(c)), including options [2][1(c)(1)(ii)]. The sources also say the head of the agency may increase the micro-purchase and simplified acquisition thresholds when supplies or services are to be used to support a contingency operation or to facilitate defense/recovery from certain events (e.g., cyber, nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attack) [4(b)–(c); 8(a)–(b)].

question: How many days before issuing a solicitation must a notice of proposed contract action be published?
key_facts: at least 15 days
answer: At least 15 days before issuance of a solicitation [1]. Exceptions: for acquisitions of commercial products or commercial services, the contracting officer may establish a shorter period or use the combined synopsis and solicitation procedure [1]. For acquisitions covered by the WTO GPA or a Free Trade Agreement, the period between synopsis publication and receipt of offers must be no less than 40 days (but may be reduced to as few as 10 days if the acquisition is within a published annual forecast) [3].

question: When is a contracting officer not required to publish a synopsis of a proposed contract action?
key_facts: list of exceptions
answer: A contracting officer need not publish the synopsis required by 5.201 when an exception in 5.202 applies.  Under 5.202(a) this includes when the contracting officer determines that any of the following conditions exist: (1) the synopsis cannot be worded without compromising national security; (2) the proposed contract action is made under the conditions described in 6.302-2 (or, for simplified acquisitions, unusual and compelling urgency precludes competition to the maximum extent practicable) and the Government would be seriously injured if the agency complied with the time periods in 5.203; (3) acquisition is required by written direction of a foreign government or by terms of an international agreement to be from specified sources; (4) the action is expressly authorized or required by statute to be made through another Government agency or a specific source (e.g., SBA 8(a) or a workshop for the blind); (5) the action is for utility services (other than telecommunications) and only one source is available; (6) the action is an order placed under subpart 16.5; (7) the action results from acceptance of a proposal under the Small Business Innovation Development Act of 1982; (8) the action results from acceptance of an unsolicited research proposal where publication would improperly disclose originality or proprietary information; (9) the action is for perishable subsistence supplies and advance notice is not appropriate or reasonable; and (10) the action is made under conditions described in 6.302-3, 6.302-5 (with regard to brand name commercial products for authorized resale), or 6.302-7 and advance notice is not appropriate or reasonable.  Additionally, FAR 13.105 reiterates that synopsis/posting requirements of 5.101 and 5.203 need not be followed when an exception in 5.202 applies, and FAR 18.103 notes that synopsis need not be submitted when there is unusual and compelling urgency and the Government would be seriously injured if the agency complied with the notice time periods (see 5.202(a)(2)).

question: When may a time-and-materials contract be used?
key_facts: only when not possible to estimate extent/duration or costs with confidence; D&F required
answer: A time-and-materials contract may be used only when “it is not possible at the time of placing the contract to estimate accurately the extent or duration of the work or to anticipate costs with any reasonable degree of confidence.” [1] In addition, a contracting officer must prepare a determination and findings that no other contract type is suitable (signed prior to execution of the base period or any option periods), the contract must include a ceiling price, and if the base period plus any option periods exceeds three years the determination must be approved by the head of the contracting activity prior to execution of the base period. [1][2][3]

question: When is a firm-fixed-price contract appropriate?
key_facts: reasonably definite specifications, fair and reasonable price can be established
answer: A firm-fixed-price contract is the standard contract form to acquire construction: "firm-fixed-price contracts shall be used to acquire construction" and may be priced "(1) on a lump-sum basis..., (2) on a unit-price basis..., or (3) using a combination of the two methods." Lump-sum pricing is preferred except when any of the listed exceptions apply: (1) large quantities of work, (2) quantities cannot be estimated with sufficient confidence, (3) estimated quantities may change significantly during construction, or (4) offerors would have to expend unusual effort to develop adequate estimates [1]. (By contrast, a fixed-price incentive contract is appropriate when a firm-fixed-price contract is not suitable) [3].

question: When must the Certificate of Independent Price Determination be included in a solicitation?
key_facts: firm-fixed-price or FPEPA contracts, with exceptions
answer: The Certificate of Independent Price Determination must be inserted in solicitations when a firm-fixed-price contract or fixed-price contract with economic price adjustment is contemplated, unless—(a) the acquisition is to be made under the simplified acquisition procedures in Part 13; (b) the solicitation is a request for technical proposals under two-step sealed bidding procedures; or (c) the solicitation is for utility services for which rates are set by law or regulation. (If the solicitation is a Request for Quotations, the terms Quotation and Quoter may be substituted for Offer and Offeror.) [1][2][6]

question: When must a contracting officer set aside an acquisition for small businesses?
key_facts: rule of two: reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small businesses at fair market prices
answer: A contracting officer shall set aside an individual acquisition or a class of acquisitions for competition among small businesses when: (a) “It is determined to be in the interest of maintaining or mobilizing the Nation's full productive capacity, war or national defense programs”; or (b) “Assuring that a fair proportion of Government contracts in each industry is placed with small business concerns” and the circumstances in 19.502-2 or 19.502-3(a) exist [1]. The set-aside requirement does not apply to purchases “at or below the micro-purchase threshold,” or purchases from required sources under part 8 [1]. Additional dollar-threshold rules: each acquisition with an anticipated dollar value “above the micro-purchase threshold, but not over the simplified acquisition threshold, shall be set aside for small business” unless the CO determines there is not a reasonable expectation of obtaining offers from two or more responsible small business concerns competitive in fair market price, quality, and delivery [2]. For acquisitions “over the simplified acquisition threshold,” the CO “shall set aside any acquisition for small business participation when there is a reasonable expectation that (1) Offers will be obtained from at least two responsible small business concerns; and (2) Award will be made at fair market prices” [2]. When a total set-aside is not appropriate, the CO must partially set aside portions (including for multiple-award contracts where authorized) only if the requirement can be divided into distinct portions, the acquisition is not subject to simplified acquisition procedures, two or more responsible small businesses are reasonably expected to submit offers competitive in price, quality, and delivery, and program eligibility requirements apply; the solicitation must identify set-aside portions and how offers are to be submitted [7][5]. No separate justification under Part 6 is required to set aside a solicitation for small business, and Subpart 19.5 prescribes the procedures to follow [8]. If a small business set-aside acquisition or portion is not awarded, the set-aside is automatically dissolved for the unawarded portion [6].

question: What are the limitations on subcontracting for a small business set-aside?
key_facts: percentage limits on amounts paid to non-similarly-situated subcontractors
answer: A small business subject to the limitations on subcontracting must meet percentage limits on the amount paid to subcontractors that are not "similarly situated entities": for services (except construction), the concern will not pay more than 50 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance to such subcontractors; for supplies/products (excluding cost of materials), the concern will not pay more than 50 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance to such subcontractors; for general construction, the concern will not pay more than 85 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance, excluding the cost of materials, to such subcontractors; and for construction by special trade contractors, the concern will not pay more than 75 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance, excluding the cost of materials, to such subcontractors. Any work that a similarly situated entity further subcontracts counts toward the small business’s applicable subcontract percentage limit. A similarly situated entity is a first-tier subcontractor (including an independent contractor) that has the same small business program status as the prime and is small under the NAICS code assigned to the subcontract. Compliance is required either by the end of the base term (and each option period) or by the end of the performance period for orders, as specified in the regulation. Independent contractors are considered subcontractors.

question: When does a contracting officer have to obtain certified cost or pricing data?
key_facts: above the $2,000,000 threshold unless an exception in 15.403-1(b) applies
answer: A contracting officer must obtain certified cost or pricing data when the contracting officer concludes that none of the exceptions in 15.403-1(b) applies and the pricing action is expected to exceed the certified-cost-or-pricing-data threshold (the threshold is $950,000 for prime contracts awarded before July 1, 2018, and $2.5 million for prime contracts awarded on or after July 1, 2018) [5][7]. When certified cost or pricing data are required, the contracting officer shall require the contractor to submit the certified cost or pricing data and a Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data in the format at 15.406-2 and include the executed certificate in the contract file [5][8]. The contracting officer may, however, consider a waiver under the exception at 15.403-1(b)(4) if exceptional circumstances exist and sufficient data are available to determine a fair and reasonable price [7]. The contracting officer must also ensure certified cost or pricing data are obtained before awards, subcontracts, or contract modifications that are expected to exceed the applicable threshold, unless an exception applies [7]. Additionally, the contracting officer shall specify in the solicitation whether certified cost or pricing data are required and related submission requirements [1].

question: What are the exceptions to requiring certified cost or pricing data?
key_facts: adequate price competition, prices set by law or regulation, commercial products/services, waiver, modifications of commercial
answer:
Exceptions described in the provided sources include: 
- Price established or controlled by law or regulation (offeror may request an exception and must identify the controlling law/regulation) [1].
- Commercial product/commercial service exception: offeror may request an exception and must, at a minimum, provide information on prior commercial sales (catalog prices, market quotations, discounts, sales history, etc.) adequate to evaluate price reasonableness; for items on an active Federal Supply Service Multiple Award Schedule, proof that an exception has been granted for the schedule item may be submitted [1][5].
- The exercise of an option at the price established at contract award or initial negotiation [3].
- Proposals used solely for overrun funding or interim billing price adjustments [3].
- Situations of adequate price competition generally do not require certified cost or pricing data (though unusual circumstances may still require additional data) [4][5].
- Head-of-contracting-activity waivers/authorizations may allow certified cost or pricing data to be obtained below the statutory threshold (see 15.403-1(b) and 15.403-1(b)(4) references) when justified [6][7].

Sources do not include the full text of FAR 15.403-1, so any other exceptions stated there (and the complete wording of 15.403-1(b)) are not listed here.

question: What standards must a prospective contractor meet to be determined responsible?
key_facts: adequate financial resources, able to meet delivery schedule, satisfactory performance record, integrity and ethics, etc.
answer: A prospective contractor must meet the general standards in FAR 9.104-1: (a) adequate financial resources or the ability to obtain them; (b) ability to comply with the required delivery or performance schedule; (c) a satisfactory performance record (lack of relevant history alone does not automatically make a contractor nonresponsible except as provided in 9.104-2); (d) a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics; (e) necessary organization, experience, accounting and operational controls, and technical skills, or the ability to obtain them; (f) necessary production, construction, and technical equipment and facilities, or the ability to obtain them; and (g) otherwise qualified and eligible to receive award under applicable laws and regulations [1]. The contracting officer must make an affirmative determination of responsibility; absent information clearly indicating responsibility, the officer must determine nonresponsibility [8]. In applying those standards, the officer may require acceptable evidence that the offeror can obtain needed resources (for example, commitments or arrangements that will exist at award) [2(a)]; a contractor seriously deficient in past performance is presumed nonresponsible unless circumstances or corrective action justify otherwise [2(b)]; the officer must consider affiliates’ or joint ventures’ past performance and integrity where relevant [2(c)]; prospective primes are generally responsible for determining subcontractor responsibility (the Government may directly determine subcontractor responsibility when in its interest) [5]; and special rules apply for small businesses (referral to SBA for Certificates of Competency and possible nonresponsibility for inability to meet limitations on subcontracting) [6].

question: What are the rules for filing a protest with the agency, and how long does an offeror have to go to GAO after an adverse agency decision?
key_facts: agency protest procedures; GAO within 10 days of knowledge of initial adverse agency action
answer:
File the protest at the agency level only after trying to resolve concerns at the contracting‑officer level; protests should be concise, logically presented, addressed to the contracting officer (or official designated in the solicitation), and must include: name/address/phone of protester; solicitation or contract number; a detailed statement of legal and factual grounds and resulting prejudice; copies of relevant documents; request for a ruling; form of relief requested; information establishing that the protester is an interested party; and information establishing timeliness. Protests based on apparent improprieties in a solicitation must be filed before bid opening or the closing date for proposals; all other agency protests must be filed no later than 10 days after the basis of protest is known or should have been known (the agency may consider untimely protests for good cause or if issues are significant). Protests may request independent review above the contracting officer per agency procedures. [2] [2] [2]

If the agency issues an adverse agency action (including an initial adverse agency decision), any subsequent protest to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) must be filed "within 10 days of knowledge of initial adverse agency action" (see 4 CFR 21.2(a)(3) as referenced). [2]

question: What must a contracting officer do before exercising an option?
key_facts: written notice, determine option is most advantageous, funds available, requirement still exists
answer: Before exercising an option the contracting officer must: 1) provide written notice to the contractor within the time period specified in the contract [2]; 2) if the contract provides for economic price adjustment and the contractor requests a revision, determine the effect of the adjustment on option prices before exercising the option [2]; 3) determine that funds are available; the requirement fulfills an existing Government need; exercise is the most advantageous method (price and other factors considered); the option was synopsized as required; the contractor has no active exclusion in SAM; past performance on other actions has been considered; and the contractor's performance on this contract has been acceptable [2]; 4) make a written determination for the contract file that exercise is in accordance with the terms of the option, the requirements of FAR 17.207 and part 6 (including that the option was evaluated as part of the initial competition and is exercisable at an amount specified in or reasonably determinable from the basic contract) [1]; and 5) notify the contractor of the exercise by a contract modification or other written document that cites the option clause as authority [1].

question: What are a contracting officer's responsibilities regarding organizational conflicts of interest?
key_facts: identify and evaluate early; avoid, neutralize, or mitigate before award
answer:
Contracting officers must—
- Analyze planned acquisitions early to identify and evaluate potential organizational conflicts of interest and to avoid, neutralize, or mitigate significant potential conflicts before award [1].
- Obtain the advice of counsel and assistance of appropriate technical specialists when evaluating potential conflicts and developing solicitation provisions and contract clauses [1].
- Before issuing a solicitation for an acquisition that may involve a significant potential conflict, recommend to the head of the contracting activity a course of action for resolving the conflict [1].
- Avoid creating unnecessary delays, burdensome information requirements, and excessive documentation; formally document their judgment only when a substantive issue concerning a potential organizational conflict of interest exists [1].
- Award the contract to the apparent successful offeror unless a conflict that cannot be avoided or mitigated is determined to exist; if withholding award for COI, notify the contractor, provide reasons, and allow a reasonable opportunity to respond [1].
- If in the Government’s best interest to award notwithstanding a conflict, submit a waiver request in accordance with 9.503 and include the waiver request and decision in the contract file [1].
- Seek necessary information from Government and readily available non‑Government sources when identifying/evaluating potential organizational conflicts of interest [4].
- If a particular acquisition involves a significant potential COI, before issuing the solicitation, submit for approval to the chief of the contracting office a written analysis with a recommended course of action, a draft solicitation provision, and, if appropriate, a proposed contract clause [4].
- Include approved provision(s) and clause(s) in the solicitation or contract, consider contractor‑provided information during solicitation or negotiations, and before award resolve the conflict consistent with the approving official’s decision [4].
- Notify a successor contracting office of any restriction if acquisition responsibility is transferred during the effective period of the restriction and send a copy of the imposing contract [4].
- Comply with subpart 9.5 before awarding a contract to an organization owned or substantially owned or controlled by Government employees [2].
Conditions/Scope: These responsibilities implement the subpart that prescribes rules, procedures, and examples for identifying, evaluating, and resolving organizational conflicts of interest and apply to contracts with profit or nonprofit organizations; they are not limited to particular kinds of acquisitions, though COIs are more likely in certain service and technical work [5][8].
